title: Stable plus construction for finite-field K-theory
notes: For \(G_n=GL_n(\mathbb F_q)\), the notes enlarge \(K(G_n,1)\) to \(B_n\), kill the commutator subgroup, fill the resulting two-dimensional cycles, and write \(K_i(G_n)=\pi_i(B_n)\). The enlarged space is called an \(H\)-space.
statement: Put \(G=\operatorname*{colim}_n GL_n(\mathbb F_q)\), and let \(E=[G,G]\), the stable elementary subgroup. The plus construction \(BG\to BG^+\) kills the perfect normal subgroup \(E\) and preserves integral homology, indeed homology with local coefficients pulled back from \(G/E\). For \(i\geq1\), \(K_i(\mathbb F_q)=\pi_i(BG^+)\). Block sum supplies the stable \(H\)-space structure. The construction can be made by attaching cells in dimensions two and three.
reconstruction: The stable group, the perfectness condition, and the distinction between attaching three-cells and ``three-cycles'' are supplied. No claim that a fixed finite \(n\) computes all higher \(K\)-groups is retained.
fate: The construction and its role in finite-field \(K\)-theory were already announced at the 1970 ICM and printed in 1971 \citep[Section 3, p. 50]{quillen1971cohomology}. The full Annals treatment appeared in November 1972 \citep{quillen1972finitefields}; the later publication does not make this a post-seminar discovery.
present_status: As of November 2026, the stable construction is standard. Fixed-rank spaces require a specified stability range, absent from the notebook.

title: Adams operations represented on reduced complex K-theory
notes: The power sum \(\sum_i\lambda_i^k\) of eigenvalues of a unitary matrix is a virtual character. It defines \(\psi^k\) on bundles and hence a self-map of \(BU\); the notes write \(K^0(X)=[X,BU]\), with a marginal qualification about quotienting trivial bundles.
statement: For a pointed connected finite CW complex, \(\widetilde K^0(X)\cong[X,BU]_*\); unreduced \(K^0\) is represented by \(\mathbb Z\times BU\). For \(k\geq1\), Newton polynomials in the exterior-power operations define a natural ring endomorphism \(\psi^k\), characterized on line bundles by \(\psi^k[L]=[L^{\otimes k}]\). The character on a rank-\(n\) bundle is the indicated power sum.
reconstruction: Reduced theory and a finite-CW domain are made explicit; a virtual representation need not be an actual bundle of nonnegative rank.
fate: Adams operations were established before 1972 and are treated in \citet[Chapter II]{atiyah1967ktheory}. Kazhdan is using this existing apparatus in Quillen's calculation.
present_status: As of November 2026, the construction and normalization remain standard; the rank component must be included for unreduced theory.

title: Finite-field K-theory as the fibre of an Adams operation
notes: The claim is \(E\psi^q=B_n=B\) ``for large \(n\)'', where \(E\psi^q\) is the fibre of \(\psi^q-1:BU\to BU\). Frobenius is identified with the topological Adams operation.
statement: For a prime power \(q\), the stable space \(BGL(\mathbb F_q)^+\) has the homotopy type of \(\operatorname{hofib}(\psi^q-1:BU\to BU)\). Since \(\psi^q\) acts on \(\pi_{2j}(BU)\cong\mathbb Z\) by multiplication by \(q^j\), its fibre has \(\pi_{2j-1}\cong\mathbb Z/(q^j-1)\) and \(\pi_{2j}=0\) for \(j\geq1\).
reconstruction: ``Fibre'' means homotopy fibre, and the equality is a homotopy equivalence after stabilization. The long exact homotopy sequence explains the numerical result rather than assuming a fixed-rank identification.
fate: The construction and its role in finite-field \(K\)-theory were already announced at the 1970 ICM and printed in 1971 \citep[Section 3, Theorem 1, p. 51]{quillen1971cohomology}. The full Annals treatment appeared in November 1972 \citep{quillen1972finitefields}; the later publication does not make this a post-seminar discovery.
present_status: As of November 2026, the equivalence and resulting finite-field groups are established; the manuscript's finite-rank shorthand remains unsafe without a stability bound.

title: A homotopy fibre does not represent the bare fixed subgroup
notes: The notes assert that \([K(X)]^k=\{\xi:\psi^k\xi=\xi\}\) is represented by \([X,E\psi^k]\), and call this easy to check.
statement: Let \(F_k=\operatorname{hofib}(\psi^k-1:BU\to BU)\). For finite pointed CW complexes there is an exact sequence of abelian groups \[\widetilde K^{-1}(X)\xrightarrow{\psi^k-1}\widetilde K^{-1}(X)\longrightarrow[X,F_k]_*\longrightarrow\widetilde K^0(X)\xrightarrow{\psi^k-1}\widetilde K^0(X).\] Thus a map into \(F_k\) includes a chosen homotopy from \(\psi^k\xi\) to \(\xi\). For \(X=S^1\) and \(k>2\), the fixed subgroup in reduced degree zero is zero, whereas \([S^1,F_k]_*\cong\mathbb Z/(k-1)\).
reconstruction: \ours{} The exact sequence and the circle counterexample are an editorial check of the literal assertion. They use \(\psi^k\) acting by \(k\) on \(\widetilde K^{-1}(S^1)\cong\widetilde K^0(S^2)\).
fate: The distinction follows from the ordinary homotopy-fibre sequence and the pre-existing Adams-operation formalism in \citet{atiyah1967ktheory}. It is not an unresolved part of Quillen's theorem.
present_status: As of November 2026, the literal representability statement is false; retaining the null-homotopy data repairs it.

title: Brauer lifting and Frobenius invariance
notes: Choose \(\mu:\overline{\mathbb F}_q^*\to\mathbb C^*\), form \(\varphi_\mu(g)=\sum_i\mu(\lambda_i)\), and invoke Brauer's theorem to obtain a virtual character. The equality of the multisets \(\{\lambda_i\}\) and \(\{\lambda_i^q\}\) gives Adams invariance; a map is then extended over the added cells.
statement: Choose compatible lifts of roots of unity of order prime to \(p=\operatorname{char}\mathbb F_q\). Brauer lifting of the defining representation produces a stable map to complex \(K\)-theory. Frobenius invariance is the relation used to lift this map to the homotopy fibre of \(\psi^q-1\). For a unipotent matrix of size \(n\), the displayed sum of eigenvalue lifts equals \(n\), not \(1\); the corresponding reduced class has rank zero.
reconstruction: The Brauer character, its stable realization, and the coherent homotopy required for the fibre lift must be distinguished. The manuscript's pointwise character argument alone does not construct that coherence or justify extension across every cell.
fate: The construction and its role in finite-field \(K\)-theory were already announced at the 1970 ICM and printed in 1971 \citep[Section 3, pp. 50--51]{quillen1971cohomology}. The full Annals treatment appeared in November 1972 \citep{quillen1972finitefields}; the later publication does not make this a post-seminar discovery.
present_status: As of November 2026, the method is established. The claim \(\varphi_\mu=1\) on unipotents is incompatible with the displayed unnormalized rank-\(n\) formula.

title: The Lang map and étale comparison
notes: To compute the homology of \(K(G_n,1)\), the notes propose \(g\mapsto g^{-1}g^\sigma\), with \(\sigma\) Frobenius, followed by the spectral sequence of a fibration.
statement: For a connected algebraic group \(G\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), the Lang map \(L(g)=g^{-1}F(g)\) is surjective and, for smooth \(G\), is a finite étale torsor under the finite group \(G(\mathbb F_q)\) acting on the left. Applied to general linear groups, it gives an étale analogue of the fibration used in the comparison with the Adams-operation fibre. A cohomological comparison requires coefficients prime to \(p\), followed by the separate treatment implicit in the finite-field theorem.
reconstruction: The connectedness, smoothness and prime-to-characteristic qualifications are supplied. The spectral sequence is a method, not an explicit calculation recorded on this page.
fate: The construction and its role in finite-field \(K\)-theory were already announced at the 1970 ICM and printed in 1971 \citep[Section 2, pp. 48--50]{quillen1971cohomology}. The full Annals treatment appeared in November 1972 \citep{quillen1972finitefields}; the later publication does not make this a post-seminar discovery.
present_status: As of November 2026, the method is standard; the manuscript does not specify enough terms or differentials to reconstruct its entire spectral sequence independently.

title: Relative perfectness and homology-preserving abelianization
notes: The condition is \([\pi_1X,\pi_1X]=[\pi_1X,[\pi_1X,\pi_1X]]\). It is said to be necessary and sufficient for a map \(X\to Y\) inducing integral homology isomorphisms with \(\pi_1Y\) abelian.
statement: For a connected CW complex \(X\), write \(G=\pi_1X\) and \(N=[G,G]\). There is a CW complex \(Y\) and a map \(f:X\to Y\) inducing the quotient \(G\to G/N\) and an isomorphism on integral homology if and only if \([G,N]=N\). The space can be constructed by attaching two- and three-cells. This is relative perfectness, which is weaker than the perfect-kernel hypothesis \([N,N]=N\) for an acyclic plus construction.
reconstruction: Surjectivity and the specified quotient on fundamental groups are made explicit. Ordinary integral homology equivalence must not be silently strengthened to an acyclic map with all local coefficients.
fate: The exact criterion appears in \citet[Corollary 4.3]{ye2012unified}; its preprint circulated in 2011 and the journal article appeared in 2012. That later verification does not establish priority for the 1972 oral statement. The attached erratum concerns a different application, not this corollary.
present_status: As of November 2026, the criterion is established. Confusing relative perfectness with perfectness would wrongly reject the notebook's formula.

title: Simple targets and the limits of the uniqueness assertion
notes: After saying the target \(Y\) need not be unique, Fuchs adds that a simple target is unique, citing Whitehead's theorem; he recalls that an \(H\)-space is simple.
statement: A path-connected \(H\)-space is simple: its fundamental group is abelian and acts trivially on higher homotopy groups. A homology equivalence between connected simple CW complexes is a weak homotopy equivalence. This criterion proves uniqueness only after a comparison map between the proposed targets has been constructed; simplicity by itself is not the missing universal property of the preceding existence construction.
reconstruction: The first two assertions are standard precise statements. The notes do not specify the category of target maps, a universal property, or the comparison map needed to infer uniqueness; that inference is therefore left unresolved rather than identified with the usual plus-construction uniqueness theorem.
fate: The homotopy-theoretic ingredients are classical; the cited Whitehead principle is discussed in \citet[Chapters 10 and 15]{may1999concise}. No exact publication matching this particular uniqueness formulation was identified in the searches for Fuchs, simple targets and homology localization.
present_status: As of November 2026, the elementary ingredients are established, but the exact uniqueness assertion recoverable from this intervention remains under-specified; this is not a claim of an open problem.

title: The Kato–Rosenblum theorem
notes: If \(H,H_0\) are self-adjoint and \(V=H-H_0\) is nuclear, their absolutely continuous parts are unitarily equivalent.
statement: Let \(H_0\) be self-adjoint on a separable Hilbert space and let \(V=V^*\in\mathcal S_1\) be bounded trace class. Set \(H=H_0+V\) on \(D(H_0)\). The wave operators \(W_\pm(H,H_0)\) exist and are complete, and intertwine the restrictions to the absolutely continuous spectral subspaces. Thus the absolutely continuous spectral measures and multiplicity functions agree up to unitary equivalence.
reconstruction: A common-domain bounded-perturbation formulation is supplied. The conclusion does not assert equivalence of the singular spectral parts.
fate: The trace-class theorem predates the talk. A stationary proof with precisely this hypothesis is given by \citet[Theorem 1, Section 3]{birmanentina1967stationary}; Section 5 identifies the stationary and time-dependent wave operators.
present_status: As of November 2026, the theorem is standard; trace-class control is a sufficient condition for complete scattering, not a classification of singular spectra.

title: Which spectral types admit trace-class-close realizations?
notes: Gelfand asks how to decide from a collection of spectral types whether realizations can be chosen whose difference is nuclear.
statement: Given two unitary-equivalence classes of bounded self-adjoint operators \(A\) and \(B\) on separable Hilbert spaces of the same dimension, characterize the existence of a unitary \(U\) for which \(A-UBU^*\in\mathcal S_1\). The data must include spectral multiplicity, not merely the closed spectral sets. The Kato--Rosenblum theorem gives equality of the absolutely continuous parts as a necessary condition; it alone does not settle the question.
reconstruction: Boundedness and the unitary-equivalence formulation make the phrase ``collection of spectral types'' precise. The notes do not say whether unbounded operators, a prescribed trace norm, or exact singular spectral measures are intended.
fate: \citet{careypincus1976traceclass} published a paper specifically on unitary equivalence modulo trace class in 1976. Its bibliographic record is verified, but its full two-operator criterion was not retrieved. A narrower consequence is stated explicitly by \citet[slide 8]{xiaundateddiagonalization}: every bounded purely singular self-adjoint operator on a separable Hilbert space is diagonalizable modulo a self-adjoint trace-class perturbation of arbitrarily small trace norm. This verifies substantive later progress, not every quantifier of the notebook's classification question.
present_status: As of November 2026, the subject has a dedicated later classification literature and the purely singular diagonalization case is verified indirectly. This audit has not independently checked the complete necessary-and-sufficient criterion for a prescribed pair of spectral types, and does not assert that equality of absolutely continuous parts alone suffices.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: Spectrum in the algebraic quotient by trace-class operators
notes: Gelfand asks: ``Spectrum in the quotient ring modulo the nuclear operators --- ?
statement: For a bounded operator \(T\) on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, define the spectrum of its coset in the unital algebra \(\mathcal B(\mathcal H)/\mathcal S_1\) algebraically, using two-sided invertibility. This spectrum equals the Fredholm essential spectrum. Indeed an inverse modulo \(\mathcal S_1\) is an inverse modulo compact operators; conversely a Fredholm operator has a parametrix with finite-rank errors, hence trace-class errors.
reconstruction: \ours{} This is one precise natural reading of the question, not a reconstruction of a proposed new invariant. The quotient is not a Banach algebra for the operator-norm quotient topology because \(\mathcal S_1\) is not operator-norm closed.
fate: The argument is the classical Fredholm-parametrix criterion, already available before the talk; it is included as an elementary editorial clarification of what the quotient-ring spectrum can and cannot distinguish. The surrounding scattering context is documented in \citet{birmanentina1967stationary}.
present_status: As of November 2026, under this algebraic interpretation the answer is the essential spectrum. A finer trace-class invariant would require additional structure beyond ordinary quotient-algebra invertibility.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: Sandwiched spectral derivatives and resolvent boundary values
notes: For Hilbert--Schmidt operators \(D_1,D_2\), the derivative of \(D_1E_\lambda D_2\) is nuclear almost everywhere, and \(D_1R_{\lambda+i\varepsilon}D_2\) has an almost-everywhere Hilbert--Schmidt boundary value as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
statement: Let \(H\) be self-adjoint with spectral resolution \(E\), and let \(D_1,D_2\in\mathcal S_2\). The function \(\lambda\mapsto D_1E(( -\infty,\lambda])D_2\) has bounded variation in \(\mathcal S_1\) and an almost-everywhere derivative in trace norm. For almost every real \(\lambda\), the sandwiched resolvents \(D_1(H-\lambda\mp i\varepsilon)^{-1}D_2\) have limits in \(\mathcal S_2\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). These statements do not assert an unsandwiched norm limit for the resolvent.
reconstruction: The topology of convergence, the almost-everywhere qualification and the use of a sandwiched spectral measure are made explicit.
fate: These are the auxiliary stationary-scattering facts developed in \citet[Section 2]{birmanentina1967stationary}. The notes correctly identify the Hilbert--Schmidt rigging that makes them usable.
present_status: As of November 2026, the facts remain standard tools for the stationary trace-class method.

title: A stationary formula for the intertwining operator
notes: An integral of the derivative of \((E_\lambda(I+VR_z^0)f,g)\), evaluated at \(z=\lambda\pm i0\), is proposed for \((W_\pm f,g)\). The perturbation \(V\) is factored into two Hilbert--Schmidt operators.
statement: For a self-adjoint trace-class perturbation, factor \(V\) through \(\mathcal S_2\), use boundary values of the sandwiched resolvents to define stationary wave operators on the absolutely continuous subspace, and extend by zero on its orthogonal complement. The resulting operators are partial isometries with initial space \(\mathcal H_{\rm ac}(H_0)\) and final space \(\mathcal H_{\rm ac}(H)\).
reconstruction: The notebook integral is a schematic weak formula: spectral-density differentiation, boundary evaluation and integration cannot be interchanged without the factorization estimates. The precise construction, rather than a falsely pointwise formula for every vector, is the modern statement.
fate: The construction is explicit in \citet[Section 3, formula (3.17) and Theorem 1]{birmanentina1967stationary}, five years before this talk.
present_status: As of November 2026, the stationary construction and its equivalence to time-dependent scattering are established.

title: Étale homotopy type and complex comparison
notes: An algebraic \(X\) over any field produces a complex \(C_X\); over \(\mathbb C\) it is the completion of the ordinary complex space.
statement: A locally noetherian scheme has an Artin--Mazur \(\acute{e}\)tale homotopy type in a pro-homotopy category, constructed from connected components of \(\acute{e}\)tale hypercovers. For a connected pointed scheme \(X\) of finite type over \(\mathbb C\), the canonical comparison from the classical analytic homotopy type to \(X_{\acute{e}t}\) induces an isomorphism after profinite completion. If \(X\) is additionally geometrically unibranch---in particular, if \(X\) is smooth or normal---then \(X_{\acute{e}t}\) itself is isomorphic to the profinite completion of the classical type in that pro-homotopy category.
reconstruction: The hypotheses on the scheme and its base point are supplied from the primary theorem. Finite type and geometric unibranchness have distinct roles in the two comparison statements. The notebook's informal ``homotopy type'' is not identified with an ordinary integral CW homotopy type.
fate: The construction circulated in the Harvard seminar of 1965--1966 and appeared as \citet{artinmazur1969etale}. The precise comparison is Theorem 12.9 and Corollary 12.10, pp. 142--143, read in the full primary text.
present_status: As of November 2026, the construction is a foundation of étale homotopy theory. The notebook's shorthand is recognizable but not a complete theorem statement.

title: Galois action on geometric étale homotopy
notes: Field automorphisms preserving \(X\) act on \(C_X\); for a variety defined over \(\mathbb Q\), the group is written \(\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb C\mid\mathbb Q)\).
statement: If \(X\) is defined over a field \(k\) with separable closure \(\bar k\), functoriality gives a homotopy-coherent action of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\bar k/k)\) on the geometric étale homotopy type of \(X_{\bar k}\). For pointed homotopy groups, a geometric point and base-point transport are required; the fundamental-group action is naturally outer until those choices are made.
reconstruction: The arithmetic Galois group and the distinctions between a functorial action, an action on a chosen model, and an outer action on a fundamental group are made explicit. The huge abstract automorphism group of \(\mathbb C\) is not treated as a group of continuous automorphisms of the analytic space.
fate: The arithmetic action is already discussed in the introduction, especially p. 4, of \citet{artinmazur1969etale}; its functorial construction belongs to their 1965--1966 seminar work published in 1969. The pointed-versus-outer-action distinction is our explicit formulation of the base-point issue.
present_status: As of November 2026, Galois actions on geometric étale homotopy types are established; the model and base-point qualifications remain essential.

title: Completion is represented in a pro-homotopy category
notes: The notes collect maps from \(X\) to spaces with finite homotopy groups and say that a compatible mapping functor is represented by \(\widehat X\).
statement: Profinite homotopy completion is characterized by maps into finite homotopy types, ordinarily meaning spaces with finitely many components, finitely many nonzero homotopy groups and each homotopy group finite. The universal object belongs to a pro-homotopy category. Maps from a test object into an inverse system and maps from an inverse system into a test object have different limit/colimit formulas; they must not be conflated.
reconstruction: The finite-type test category and pro-representability are a reconstruction. The notebook's product of compatible \(\operatorname{Hom}(Y,X_i)\) describes maps to a given pro-system, not by itself the universal construction of the completion of \(X\).
fate: The pro-category and completion are constructed in \citet[Sections 2--3, pp. 20--34]{artinmazur1969etale}; the complex comparison is Theorem 12.9. This is prior foundational work, not a conjectural completion procedure first proposed in the seminar.
present_status: As of November 2026, the pro-categorical formulation is standard. Ordinary representability by one cell complex is not justified by the text.

title: Time-dependent wave operators, intertwining and completeness
notes: The strong limits \(W_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}e^{itH}e^{-itH_0}P_0\) are defined, with \(P_0\) the absolutely continuous projection. The notes state \(W_\pm H_0=HW_\pm\) and say completeness is equivalent to existence of the reverse wave operator.
statement: For self-adjoint \(H,H_0\), if the indicated strong limit exists, it is an isometry on \(\mathcal H_{\rm ac}(H_0)\), vanishes on its orthogonal complement, and intertwines bounded Borel functions of the operators. It is complete precisely when the corresponding reverse wave operator exists and has adjoint \(W_\pm(H,H_0)^*\). Under the common-domain trace-class perturbation hypothesis, existence holds in both directions and hence completeness follows.
reconstruction: The adjoint relation and the spectral-projection meaning of the unbounded intertwining identity are supplied. Existence alone is not completeness for arbitrary nonsymmetric hypotheses.
fate: These are established scattering-theory facts; \citet[Sections 1 and 5]{birmanentina1967stationary} give the stationary/time-dependent comparison used in the talk.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statements are standard with the stated absolutely continuous projections and domains.

title: The chain rule for wave operators
notes: The displayed composition is \(W_\pm(H_3,H_2)W_\pm(H_2,H_1)=W_\pm(H_3,H_1)\).
statement: Let \(H_1,H_2,H_3\) be self-adjoint on the same Hilbert space, and use the ordinary wave operators \(W_\pm(H_j,H_i)=\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\pm\infty}e^{itH_j}e^{-itH_i}P_{\rm ac}(H_i)\). If \(W_\pm(H_3,H_2)\) and \(W_\pm(H_2,H_1)\) exist for a fixed sign, then \(W_\pm(H_3,H_1)\) exists and equals their product. The range of the second factor lies in \(\mathcal H_{\rm ac}(H_2)\), which permits insertion of the intermediate projection. Completeness of both factors implies completeness of the product.
reconstruction: A fixed common sign is required. The insertion of the intermediate absolutely continuous projection is the point that makes the strong-limit multiplication legitimate.
fate: The chain rule belongs to the general wave-operator framework summarized in \citet[Section 1]{birmanentina1967stationary}; it is not a new consequence first obtained in 1972.
present_status: As of November 2026, the chain rule remains valid in this setting and is frequently used to reduce perturbation comparisons to intermediate operators.

title: Resolvent factorization and spectral localization of the stationary formula
notes: With \(Q_z=I+VR_z^0\), Birman writes \(R_z^0-R_{\bar z}^0=Q_z^*(R_z-R_{\bar z})Q_z\). The upper integration bound \(\sigma\) gives \((E_\sigma W_\pm f,g)\), and the construction is independent of the Hilbert--Schmidt factorization of \(V\).
statement: Let \(H_0\) be self-adjoint, \(V=V^*\in\mathcal S_1\), and \(H=H_0+V\) on \(D(H_0)\). For \(z\notin\mathbb R\), put \(R_z=(H-z)^{-1}\), \(R_z^0=(H_0-z)^{-1}\), and \(Q_z=I+VR_z^0\). The resolvent identity gives \(R_zQ_z=R_z^0\). Combining this with \(R_z-R_{\bar z}=(z-\bar z)R_z^*R_z\) gives \(R_z^0-R_{\bar z}^0=Q_z^*(R_z-R_{\bar z})Q_z\). After Hilbert--Schmidt sandwiching and almost-everywhere boundary passage, this identifies the absolutely continuous spectral densities and makes the stationary partial isometry respect spectral projections. Uniqueness of the resulting weak form yields independence of the factorization.
reconstruction: The formula is checked with the notes' resolvent convention. A density statement is made only after rigging; it is not an operator-norm identity for unsandwiched boundary resolvents.
fate: The argument is the stationary proof in \citet[Section 3, Theorem 1]{birmanentina1967stationary}, the paper explicitly named in the notebook.
present_status: As of November 2026, the derivation is established and the resolvent identity is correct with this convention.

title: Birman’s local trace-class criterion with domain control
notes: The ``more general variant'' asks for \(E(\Delta)(H-H_0)E_0(\Delta)\in\mathcal S_1\), followed by a comparison of domains of growing functions of \(H\) and \(H_0\). The inclusion sign and the functions are not fully resolved.
statement: Let \(H,H_0\) be self-adjoint operators on a separable Hilbert space, with spectral projections \(E,E_0\). Assume that, for every bounded interval \(\Delta\), the bounded operator \[H E(\Delta)E_0(\Delta)-E(\Delta)H_0E_0(\Delta)\] belongs to the trace class. Assume also that there exist real Borel functions \(f,f_0\), bounded on compact intervals and satisfying \(|f(\lambda)|,|f_0(\lambda)|\to\infty\) as \(|\lambda|\to\infty\), such that \(D(f(H))=D(f_0(H_0))\). Then both time-dependent wave operators exist and are complete. The domain equality is a sufficient form of the mutual-subordination hypothesis in Birman's theorem.
reconstruction: The scan does contain the equality of the two functional-calculus domains and the statement that the functions grow at infinity. Borel measurability, local boundedness and absolute growth are made explicit. The localized difference is written as the bounded expression above so that no undefined subtraction on unequal operator domains is needed. Birman's Definition 4.2 allows one domain inclusion for subordination; mutual subordination follows from the displayed equality.
fate: This is the local criterion of \citet[Definition 4.2 and Theorem 4.4, pp. 897--900]{birman1968local}, received 23 January 1968 and published that year. Its hypotheses are more general than a globally trace-class difference and explain precisely the final lines of the 27 March lecture.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established scattering theorem. The notebook's compressed domain condition can be reconstructed from the 1968 source; no separate open extension is justified.

title: Grothendieck covering families and fibre products
notes: Coverings are families \(\{X_\alpha\to X\}\), stable under isomorphisms, composition and arbitrary base change. The base-change axiom explicitly requires existence of \(X_\alpha\times_X U\); a universal diagram defines the fibre product.
statement: A pretopology on a category \(T\) assigns covering families satisfying the three stated axioms. A fibre product \(U\times_XV\) represents pairs of arrows to \(U,V\) with equal composites to \(X\). The associated Grothendieck topology consists of sieves containing a covering family. The distinction between a pretopology and its topology matters when different covering families generate the same sheaves.
reconstruction: The modern term pretopology and the associated-sieve construction are supplied; the manuscript's axioms themselves are accurate.
fate: The framework was circulated in SGA 4 in 1963--64 and published in 1972 \citep{sga41972topos}; a precise current formulation is \citet[Tag 00VH]{stacks2026sites}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the definitions are standard and recur from the seminar's earlier years.

title: Presheaves, natural transformations and the functor category
notes: A presheaf is a contravariant functor \(T\to A\), with \(A\) abelian. A commuting square defines a morphism of functors; the notes observe a possible set-theoretic size issue.
statement: For a small site \(T\), an abelian presheaf is a functor \(T^{\rm op}\to\mathbf{Ab}\). A morphism consists of maps \(t_U:F(U)\to G(U)\) commuting with every restriction map. These form an abelian functor category with kernels and cokernels computed objectwise. For a large site, one fixes a universe or a suitable small presentation before asserting that morphism collections are sets.
reconstruction: The coefficient category is restricted to abelian groups in the statements used below. Mere existence of infinite direct sums in an arbitrary abelian category is not a complete substitute for all limits and exactness conditions needed in the subsequent sheaf theory.
fate: This is the categorical language of \citet[Chapter I]{grothendieck1957homological} and \citet[Expos\'e I]{sga41972topos}. The seminar is building shared terminology.
present_status: As of November 2026, these constructions are standard; the manuscript's warning about size is appropriate.

title: The sheaf condition uses products over an arbitrary cover
notes: The sheaf condition is displayed with \(\bigoplus_\alpha F(X_\alpha)\) and \(\bigoplus_{\alpha,\beta}F(X_\alpha\times_X X_\beta)\), although the covering index is an arbitrary set.
statement: For every covering \(\{U_i\to U\}\), an abelian presheaf is a sheaf when \[0\longrightarrow F(U)\longrightarrow\prod_iF(U_i)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{pr}_1^*-\operatorname{pr}_2^*}\prod_{i,j}F(U_i\times_UU_j)\] is exact. Products and direct sums coincide for finite covers, but direct sums impose an unwarranted finite-support condition on infinite covers.
reconstruction: \ours{} The products are an emendation of the mathematical statement, not a silent change to the diplomatic transcription. For an infinite discrete space covered by its points, a global locally constant function need not have finite support.
fate: The exact equalizer formulation is \citet[Tag 00VM]{stacks2026sites}; it belongs to the pre-existing sheaf formalism of SGA 4.
present_status: As of November 2026, the arbitrary-cover statement in the notebook is false with direct sums and correct with products.

title: Sheafification, adjunction and the abelian category of sheaves
notes: The full subcategory \(S_T\) of sheaves is abelian. The proof uses an associated-sheaf functor \(\#\), adjoint to the inclusion \(i:S_T\to P_T\). Adjointness is defined by a natural Hom-set isomorphism.
statement: For abelian presheaves on a small site, sheafification \(a:P_T\to S_T\) is an exact left adjoint to the inclusion: \(\operatorname{Hom}(aF,G)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(F,iG)\), naturally in both variables. The category \(S_T\) is abelian; kernels are computed as presheaf kernels, whereas cokernels must be sheafified. A Hom-set bijection without naturality would not define an adjunction.
reconstruction: The direction of the adjunction and exactness of sheafification are explicit. The conclusion is stated for abelian groups, the coefficient category actually needed later.
fate: These results are in the classical site formalism \citep{sga41972topos}; \citet[Tag 03CM, Lemmas 18.3.1--2]{stacks2026foundations} verifies the exact current statements.
present_status: As of November 2026, the theorem and proof mechanism are standard; inclusion of sheaves into presheaves is generally only left exact.

title: Cohomology on a site as a derived section functor
notes: The definition is \(H^q(T,X,F)=R^qi(F)(X)\), where \(i\) includes sheaves in presheaves.
statement: For an object \(X\) of a small site and an abelian sheaf \(F\), define \(H^q(X,F)=R^q\Gamma(X,-)(F)\). Abelian sheaves have enough injectives. Evaluation of presheaves at \(X\) is exact, so computing an injective resolution also gives \(H^q(X,F)=(R^qi(F))(X)\).
reconstruction: Enough injectives and the exactness of evaluation explain why the notebook's seemingly unusual inclusion-functor definition agrees with ordinary site cohomology.
fate: The homological construction predates the talk \citep{grothendieck1957homological}; the site version and enough-injectives theorem are verified in \citet[Tags 01DL and 03NT]{stacks2026foundations}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the definition is correct for abelian sheaves on a site, with standard size conventions.

title: Continuity of a functor of sites
notes: A morphism of topologies is defined as a functor carrying coverings to coverings; precomposition \(F\mapsto F\circ f\) is asserted to carry sheaves to sheaves.
statement: If \(f:T_1\to T_2\) carries covering families to covering families and preserves the fibre products that occur in their descent diagrams, then precomposition carries sheaves on \(T_2\) to sheaves on \(T_1\). More generally continuity is defined by that sheaf-preservation condition. Cover preservation alone does not justify substituting \(f(U_i\times_UU_j)\) for \(f(U_i)\times_{f(U)}f(U_j)\).
reconstruction: The missing fibre-product compatibility is supplied. The direction and notation in the notes are retained as precomposition, without identifying this automatically with the exact inverse-image functor of a geometric morphism of topoi.
fate: The distinction is part of \citet[Expos\'e III]{sga41972topos}. Its 1963--64 circulation predates the seminar; the volume appeared in 1972.
present_status: As of November 2026, the construction is standard under continuity hypotheses, while the displayed definition is insufficient as written.

title: Grothendieck and Leray spectral sequences
notes: For \(A\xrightarrow F B\xrightarrow G C\), the notes state \(R^pG\,R^qF\Rightarrow R^{p+q}(GF)\) ``under certain conditions'', and present the site Leray sequence as a special case.
statement: Let \(A,B,C\) be abelian categories, with enough injectives in \(A,B\). Suppose \(F,G\) are additive left exact functors and \(F\) carries injectives to \(G\)-acyclic objects. For \(M\in A\), there is a first-quadrant spectral sequence \(E_2^{p,q}=R^pG(R^qF(M))\Rightarrow R^{p+q}(GF)(M)\). For a morphism of topoi \(f\), this yields \(H^p(Y,R^qf_*F)\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(X,F)\).
reconstruction: The acyclicity assumption is the decisive missing condition. The modern Leray formulation uses the direct-image functor \(f_*\); the manuscript's opposite site-functor conventions must be translated before comparing symbols.
fate: The composite-functor spectral sequence is due to the earlier homological formalism \citep{grothendieck1957homological}; its hypotheses and convergence are verified in \citet[Tag 015L, Lemma 13.22.2]{stacks2026foundations}. The earlier site formulation is also explicit in \citet[Chapter II, Theorem 4.11]{artin1962topologies}, read in the 1962 primary notes.
present_status: As of November 2026, the spectral sequence is established. Exactness of precomposition on presheaves alone does not replace the injective-acyclicity check on sheaves.

title: Group objects and the classifying site
notes: A group object is described by a functorial group structure on \(h_G(Y)\), or by multiplication, inversion and a unit. The new site \(TG\) consists of \(G\)-objects, equivariant maps and underlying coverings; its final object is called a classifying space.
statement: In a category with finite products, a group object is an object \(G\) equipped with the group-law diagrams. Yoneda identifies this with a group structure on every \(\operatorname{Hom}(Y,G)\), natural in \(Y\). For a group object in a topos \(T\), the topos of \(G\)-objects is its classifying topos \(B_TG\). Its final object is the base's final object with trivial action; the topology and equivariance, not a nontrivial underlying terminal set, encode classifying cohomology.
reconstruction: The classifying topos is distinguished from a topological classifying space. For a discrete group over the topos of sets, abelian objects are \(G\)-modules and derived global sections recover group cohomology.
fate: The construction belongs to \citet[Expos\'e IV]{sga41972topos}. It is the conceptual language needed for the subsequent comparison, not a new construction of ordinary \(BG\) from a terminal object.
present_status: As of November 2026, the classifying-topos interpretation is standard; the notebook's terminal-object phrase is too compressed if read as a statement about ordinary spaces.

title: Constant sheaves and the local coefficients in a fibration sequence
notes: The constant sheaf associated with \(A\) is correctly obtained from the constant presheaf. A later display simplifies the \(E_2\) page to \(H^p(BG)\otimes H^q(G)\).
statement: The constant sheaf \(\underline A\) is the sheafification of the constant presheaf with value \(A\). Let \(F\to E\to B\) be a Serre fibration with connected CW base and fibre of CW type, and let \(k\) be a field. Its cohomology spectral sequence has \(E_2^{p,q}=H^p(B;\mathcal H^q(F;k))\), where monodromy defines the coefficient system. If monodromy on each \(H^q(F;k)\) is trivial and each such vector space is finite dimensional, then \(E_2^{p,q}\cong H^p(B;k)\otimes_k H^q(F;k)\).
reconstruction: The fibration version is a precise model of the analogy drawn in the notes. Trivial local coefficients and tensor-product hypotheses are supplied; no general tensor-product formula for arbitrary sites or coefficient rings is asserted. Finite-dimensional fibre cohomology in every degree is one explicit sufficient condition for the tensor identification.
fate: Constant sheaves and site Leray sequences are already present in SGA 4 \citep{sga41972topos}; the classical fibration sequence is the topological analogy used by the speaker.
present_status: As of November 2026, the constant-sheaf construction is correct. The tensor notation needs the additional conditions expressly alluded to but not specified in the notes.

title: Quillen’s mod-l cohomology of a finite general linear group
notes: The notes write \(H^*(GL_n(\mathbb F_q);\mathbb F_\ell)=S[c_1,\ldots,c_n]\otimes\Lambda[c'_1,\ldots,c'_n]\), with degrees \(2i\) and \(2i-1\), but do not state the relation between \(q\) and \(\ell\). One coefficient field is also written \(\mathbb F_q\).
statement: For an odd prime \(\ell\neq\operatorname{char}\mathbb F_q\), let \(r\) be the multiplicative order of \(q\) modulo \(\ell\), and \(m=\lfloor n/r\rfloor\). Quillen's description is \[H^*(GL_n(\mathbb F_q);\mathbb F_\ell)\cong\mathbb F_\ell[c_r,c_{2r},\ldots,c_{mr}]\otimes\Lambda(e_r,e_{2r},\ldots,e_{mr}),\] with \(|c_{jr}|=2jr\), \(|e_{jr}|=2jr-1\). The displayed notebook formula is the case \(r=1\), namely \(\ell\mid q-1\). The prime \(2\) requires separate cases.
reconstruction: The odd-prime restrictions and the order \(r\) supply the absent hypotheses. The coefficient of every cohomology group in this formula is \(\mathbb F_\ell\).
fate: The formula, including the odd-prime algebra qualification, is explicit in \citet[Section 2, p. 50]{quillen1971cohomology}, announced at ICM 1970 and printed in 1971. The fuller journal account appeared in November 1972 \citep{quillen1972finitefields}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the formula with these qualifications is established. The unrestricted printed formula is false, for example when \(\ell\nmid|GL_n(\mathbb F_q)|\), when all positive-degree cohomology vanishes.

title: Finite generation through a faithful unitary representation
notes: A faithful irreducible representation \(G\to U\) and the induced \(BG\to BU\) are invoked to explain finite generation of group cohomology.
statement: A finite group has a faithful finite-dimensional unitary representation, for example its regular representation. It need not have a faithful irreducible representation. The classical finite-generation theorem says that \(H^*(G;\mathbb F_\ell)\) is a finitely generated algebra for every finite group \(G\); the topological proof uses \(G\subset U(N)\) and the fibration \(U(N)/G\to BG\to BU(N)\).
reconstruction: Irreducibility is removed; it is false for a noncyclic finite abelian group. The coefficient ring and finiteness of \(G\) are stated explicitly.
fate: Finite generation is already attributed to Venkov and Evens in \citet[Section 1, p. 47]{quillen1971cohomology}. A modern independent proof appears in \citet[Theorem 2.4]{rouquier2014finite}. The faithful embedding need not be irreducible; the regular representation supplies an unconditional embedding of any finite group.
present_status: As of November 2026, finite generation is established. It gives no automatic explicit set of Quillen generators or a Brauer-lift comparison.

title: Comparing finite-field and complex algebraic groups
notes: Passing from \(GL_n(\mathbb F_q)\) to \(GL_n(\overline{\mathbb F}_q)\), the notes say the resulting classifying object, properly interpreted, equals \(BU\). Bernstein adds that representations over the algebraic closure and over \(\mathbb C\) are described by highest weights.
statement: The comparison concerns étale or prime-to-characteristic completed homotopy/cohomology of algebraic groups and their classifying objects, not an equality between the discrete classifying space of \(GL_n(\overline{\mathbb F}_q)\) and the ordinary topological \(BU(n)\). For a split connected reductive group over an algebraically closed field, simple rational representations are indexed by dominant highest weights. In positive characteristic their dimensions, characters and semisimplicity properties need not agree with characteristic zero.
reconstruction: The topology, finite rank and coefficient restrictions are restored. The highest-weight observation is separated from the much stronger and false assertion that the two representation categories coincide.
fate: Quillen's comparison strategy and its prime-to-characteristic coefficients were already announced in \citet[Section 2]{quillen1971cohomology}. For Bernstein's aside, \citet[Theorem 22.2 and Sections 22.3--22.5]{milne2017groups} states the characteristic-independent highest-weight parametrization for split reductive groups. It does not identify the dimensions or characters of all corresponding simple modules across characteristics.
present_status: As of November 2026, these qualified comparisons are established; neither literal equality of spaces nor characteristic-independent ordinary representation theory follows from the notebook.

title: Complexes, cohomology, degree and homotopy
notes: A complex \(0\to C_0\xrightarrow{d_0}C_1\to\cdots\) has \(H^q=\ker d_q/\operatorname{im}d_{q-1}\). Maps of degree \(\tau\) are introduced and a homotopy formula \(f-g=d\alpha+\alpha d'\) is written without consistent indices or signs.
statement: For a cochain complex \(C^\bullet\) in an abelian category, \(d^{n+1}d^n=0\) and \(H^n(C)=\ker d^n/\operatorname{im}d^{n-1}\). Degree-zero chain maps \(f,g:C\to D\) are homotopic if \(f-g=d_Dh+hd_C\), with \(h^n:C^n\to D^{n-1}\). In the graded Hom complex a degree-\(\tau\) map has differential \(d_Df-(-1)^\tau fd_C\); the corresponding signed boundary formula governs higher-degree homotopies.
reconstruction: The degree-zero statement makes the notebook's intended homotopy unambiguous. The graded sign convention is explicitly supplied rather than treating the unsigned formula as correct in every degree.
fate: These are the classical chain-complex definitions, incorporated in the derived-category formalism before 1972; see \citet[Chapter I]{hartshorne1966residues} and \citet[Chapter 12]{may1999concise}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the definitions are standard; homotopic maps induce equal maps on cohomology.

title: The homotopy category is generally not abelian
notes: Morphisms are maps modulo null-homotopic maps. The notes collect morphisms of all degrees into a direct sum, then stress that the resulting category is not abelian because of homotopy equivalence.
statement: The ordinary homotopy category \(K(A)\) has complexes as objects and homotopy classes of degree-zero chain maps as morphisms. It is additive and triangulated, but generally not abelian. The groups \(\operatorname{Hom}_{K(A)}(C,D[\tau])\) form a graded enhancement; collecting every degree changes the morphism convention and should not be confused with ordinary \(K(A)\).
reconstruction: The text's all-degrees convention is separated from the standard category used in the subsequent localization. The abelian category of actual complexes and chain maps must also be distinguished from its homotopy category.
fate: The distinction is already in \citet[Chapter I]{hartshorne1966residues}; the precise conventions are verified in \citet[Tag 03T3]{stacks2026foundations}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the non-abelian homotopy-category statement is established, with the specified convention for morphisms.

title: The derived category and its universal property
notes: The functor \(K(A)\to D(A)\) sends cohomology isomorphisms to isomorphisms, is universal with this property, and in fact a chain map becomes invertible exactly when it induces cohomology isomorphisms.
statement: Let \(S\) be the quasi-isomorphisms in \(K(A)\). The derived category is \(D(A)=K(A)[S^{-1}]\), with the localization universal property: every functor inverting \(S\) factors uniquely up to natural isomorphism through \(D(A)\). The cohomology functors descend to \(D(A)\); a map in \(K(A)\) is a quasi-isomorphism if and only if its localized image is invertible.
reconstruction: The relevant set-theoretic universe and existence of the localization are tacit; the bounded-below setting of the talk suffices in the standard module and sheaf categories.
fate: The construction was available in the 1963--64 Harvard seminar published as \citet[Chapter I]{hartshorne1966residues}; \citet[Tag 03T3]{stacks2026foundations} verifies the current convention.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is the standard derived category, and the universal property recorded in the notes is accurate.

title: Derived morphisms retain information invisible to cohomology
notes: The notes emphatically say that \(D(A)\) is not obtained by declaring \(f\sim g\) when \(f^*=g^*\); it has more morphisms, obtained by formally adjoining inverses.
statement: In general the functor \(H^*:D(A)\to\operatorname{Gr}(A)\) is not faithful. For modules, \(\operatorname{Hom}_{D(R)}(M,N[1])\cong\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(M,N)\). For example \(R=\mathbb Z\), \(M=N=\mathbb Z/p\), this group is \(\mathbb Z/p\), whereas a morphism \(M\to N[1]\) induces zero on each cohomology group because the nonzero groups lie in different degrees.
reconstruction: \ours{} The Ext example is an editorial illustration of the correct warning in the notebook; it is not presented as an example supplied by the speaker.
fate: This is an elementary consequence of the earlier derived-functor formalism \citep[Chapter I]{hartshorne1966residues}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the warning is correct and essential: cohomology detects quasi-isomorphisms without determining every morphism.

title: Roofs and the direction of the limit
notes: Morphisms from \(C\) to \(D\) are represented by diagrams \(C\leftarrow C'\to D\), with the left arrow a cohomology isomorphism. The notes call the set of such morphisms a projective limit.
statement: A morphism in \(D(A)\) is represented by a roof \(C\xleftarrow{s}C'\xrightarrow{f}D\), with \(s\) a quasi-isomorphism, modulo the calculus-of-fractions equivalence by common refinements in \(K(A)\). The Hom set is a filtered colimit of the corresponding Hom sets over quasi-isomorphic replacements, with the appropriate opposite indexing category. It is not the inverse limit of all roof diagrams.
reconstruction: The homotopy-category equivalence relation and the direction of the colimit are supplied. The word \ru{проект. предел} is visible in the scan and is treated as a mathematical emendation, not an English translation mistake.
fate: Roofs are the standard localization construction of \citet[Chapter I]{hartshorne1966residues}; they implement the universal property described correctly earlier on the same page.
present_status: As of November 2026, the roof construction is established, while the unqualified projective-limit statement needs correction.

title: When an additive functor has a total derived functor
notes: The concluding line sends \(f:A\to A'\) to \(D(f):D(A)\to D(A')\), without stating exactness or resolution hypotheses.
statement: An exact additive functor preserves quasi-isomorphisms and induces a functor on derived categories. For a left exact additive functor \(F:A\to A'\), with enough injectives in \(A\), the bounded-below right derived functor is \(RF:D^+(A)\to D^+(A')\), computed by applying \(F\) to an injective resolution. A general additive functor has no automatic induced functor on the unlocalized cohomology classes.
reconstruction: The two cases, exact functor and right derived functor, are distinguished. Kazhdan's next intervention supplies the missing injective-resolution mechanism.
fate: The construction is classical; \citet[Tag 03T3, Definition 64.6.4]{stacks2026foundations} verifies exactly the bounded-below formulation.
present_status: As of November 2026, derived functors are standard under these hypotheses; the unrestricted displayed notation suppresses necessary assumptions.

title: Bounded-below injective complexes model the derived category
notes: If \(A\) has enough injectives, the category of complexes in \(\operatorname{Inj}(A)\) is said to be equivalent to the derived category of \(A\).
statement: For an abelian category \(A\) with enough injectives, the natural functor \(K^+(\operatorname{Inj}A)\to D^+(A)\) is an equivalence. Morphisms on the left are chain maps modulo homotopy, not arbitrary chain maps. For unbounded complexes, termwise injectivity is insufficient in general; one uses \(K\)-injective resolutions in categories where they exist.
reconstruction: Bounded-below complexes and passage to homotopy classes are restored. This is the precise result compatible with the preceding nonnegative complexes.
fate: The result belongs to the pre-1972 derived-category theory \citep{hartshorne1966residues}; \citet[Tag 03T3, Lemma 64.6.3]{stacks2026foundations} states the exact equivalence.
present_status: As of November 2026, the bounded-below theorem is established. Its unbounded analogue needs the stronger \(K\)-injective condition.

title: Unoriented, oriented and stably complex bordism
notes: Closed compact smooth manifolds are equivalent when they form the boundary of a compact manifold. Unoriented bordism has \([M]+[M]=0\). A weak complex manifold includes a complex bundle \(\xi\) and a fixed stable real-bundle isomorphism with the tangent bundle.
statement: Unoriented bordism uses \(\partial W\cong M\sqcup N\) and disjoint-union addition. Oriented bordism requires \(\partial W\cong M\sqcup(-N)\). A stable complex structure on a smooth manifold is a complex structure on its stabilized tangent bundle, up to the standard stable homotopy equivalence; its choice induces an orientation and must extend across a bordism. It is data, not merely the existence of some isomorphism of underlying real bundles.
reconstruction: Boundary orientations and stable homotopies of the chosen structure are supplied. The cylinder proves exponent two only in unoriented bordism, not in complex bordism.
fate: These geometric definitions precede the talk and are the input of \citet{connerfloyd1966relation} and the complex-bordism theory used in \citet{quillen1969formal}.
present_status: As of November 2026, all three bordism theories are standard; keeping the extra structures prevents the false transfer of the unoriented exponent-two assertion.

title: Representatives by complex manifolds: a necessary qualification
notes: The notes assert that every weak complex manifold is bordant to a complex manifold.
statement: A safe precise result is that the complex bordism ring is generated, as a ring over \(\mathbb Z\), by classes of nonsingular projective varieties; hence each class is an integral linear combination of such classes. This does not mean that every class, with its specified stable complex orientation, is represented by a nonnegative disjoint union of complex manifolds. In dimension zero, \(MU_0\cong\mathbb Z\), and a negatively oriented point represents \(-1\), which no ordinary compact complex zero-manifold represents.
reconstruction: \ours{} The generated-ring statement is the verified replacement. The zero-dimensional counterexample diagnoses the universal literal wording; no assertion about the sharp positive-dimensional realization theorem is inferred from this brief line.
fate: The use of nonsingular projective generators is explicit in the proof of \citet[Theorem 2]{quillen1969formal}, relying on the earlier complex-bordism calculation.
present_status: As of November 2026, the ring-generation result is established. The unqualified literal claim has a zero-dimensional counterexample.

title: The complex bordism coefficient ring
notes: The coefficient ring is written \(\Omega_*^U=\mathbb Z[t_0,t_1,\ldots]\), with \(\deg t_i=2i\). Products are Cartesian products, and inverses require changing the stable complex structure appropriately.
statement: The complex bordism coefficient ring is \(MU_*\cong\mathbb Z[x_1,x_2,\ldots]\), where \(|x_i|=2i\) for \(i\geq1\); \(MU_0=\mathbb Z\) and \(MU_{2i+1}=0\). There is no independent degree-zero polynomial generator. Multiplication is induced by Cartesian product, with the product stable complex structure.
reconstruction: The subscript zero is removed as an independent generator; if \(t_0\) was intended to denote the point, it must equal the unit rather than a polynomial variable.
fate: The Milnor--Novikov coefficient-ring calculation predates the talk; \citet[Theorem 2 and its proof]{quillen1969formal} identifies it with Lazard's polynomial ring and uses the projective generators.
present_status: As of November 2026, the polynomial presentation is established; the notebook's extra degree-zero variable is erroneous if read literally.

title: Bordism of a space and the module-classification programme
notes: A cycle over \(X\) is \([M,\xi,\alpha,f]\) with \(f:M\to X\), and a bordism extends all the data. The direct sum \(\Omega_*^U(X)\) is an \(\Omega_*^U\)-module. A problem asks to describe its module structure.
statement: For a CW space \(X\), geometric complex bordism defines the homology theory \(MU_*(X)\). External products with coefficient manifolds make it a graded \(MU_*\)-module. The broad request to describe this module has no specified class of spaces or proposed classification invariant in the notes; it becomes a programme rather than a single quantified problem.
reconstruction: The covariant theory here is homology, despite later notation resembling \(K^*(X)\). No claim is made that all graded modules arise as \(MU_*(X)\), or that height data alone classify them.
fate: Module structures were already a focus of complex-bordism theory before 1972. \citet[Introduction and Section 3]{johnsonwilson1975operations} makes the later height-local structure results precise and explicitly builds on Morava's 1971 unpublished work.
present_status: As of November 2026, the module construction is standard, while the broad classification request is not a sufficiently bounded open problem to receive a new problem identifier.

title: Modules as quasicoherent sheaves and their fibres
notes: Ignoring most grading, the polynomial ring is viewed as the coordinate ring of an infinite affine space, and \(MU_*(X)\) as a sheaf; even and odd degrees are retained separately.
statement: Put \(L=MU_*\) and \(M=MU_*(X)\). The associated quasicoherent sheaf \(\widetilde M\) on \(\operatorname{Spec}L\) has fibre \(M\otimes_L\kappa(\mathfrak p)\) at a prime \(\mathfrak p\). Forgetting to parity preserves a \(\mathbb Z/2\)-grading but discards the full weight information. Since \(L\) has infinitely many polynomial generators, this affine scheme is not noetherian.
reconstruction: The residue-field tensor product and the distinction between a stalk and its fibre are supplied. Fibres are vector spaces over varying residue fields, so they cannot literally all be the same integral \(K\)-group.
fate: The module-to-sheaf construction is older affine algebraic geometry. Morava's use of it for formal groups is made explicit in \citet{morava1972moduli} and developed in \citet[Section 0.1]{morava1985noetherian}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the construction is standard and gives the correct language for the following geometric claims, provided the grading and base field are tracked.

title: The dense-open K-theory claim and the Conner–Floyd comparison
notes: A theorem attributed to Morava and Quillen says that every fibre over a dense open set is \(K^0(X)\oplus K^1(X)\); the open is identified with inverting \(t_1=[\mathbb {CP}^1]\).
statement: For a finite CW complex, the Conner--Floyd comparison identifies \(MU_*(X)\otimes_{MU_*}KU_*\) with \(KU_*(X)\), where the coefficient map is the multiplicative formal group law and \(KU_*=\mathbb Z[\beta^{\pm1}]\). Inverting a degree-two polynomial generator in the universal ring does not impose that coefficient map. A geometric fibre at \(\mathfrak p\) is instead a vector space over \(\kappa(\mathfrak p)\); even at \(X=\mathrm{pt}\), it is not the integral group \(K^0(\mathrm{pt})=\mathbb Z\).
reconstruction: \ours{} The comparison is stated in the covariant homology convention of the lecture. Passing to cohomology requires the corresponding finite-complex comparison, not an unmentioned identification of homology and cohomology. The height-one locus is defined prime by prime through the Hasse invariant, not by one universal \(t_1\) in all characteristics.
fate: The correctly delimited comparison predates the talk \citep{connerfloyd1966relation}; the formal-group interpretation is explained by \citet{quillen1969formal}. Later height-local theory implements Morava's broader idea, but does not vindicate the literal fibre claim.
present_status: As of November 2026, the Conner--Floyd theorem is established. The notebook's global dense-open fibre statement is false as written and should not be counted as an unsolved conjecture.

title: Formal coordinate changes and equivariant bordism data
notes: The group \(\Gamma(R)\) consists of \(f(t)=a_1t+a_2t^2+\cdots\), with \(a_1\) invertible. It acts by \(F^f(x,y)=f^{-1}F(f(x),f(y))\), and the bordism sheaf is called equivariant, ``constant on orbits''.
statement: Formal substitutions with invertible linear term form a group under composition and act on one-dimensional commutative formal group laws by the displayed formula. Strict coordinate changes have \(a_1=1\). The flat Hopf algebroid \((MU_*,MU_*MU)\) encodes formal group laws and strict isomorphisms; the grading records the additional scaling. The comodule \(MU_*(X)\) therefore has descent data. Equivariance identifies fibres along chosen isomorphisms while allowing nontrivial stabilizer actions; it does not make the sheaf canonically constant on each orbit.
reconstruction: The strict/full-coordinate distinction and stabilizer action are supplied. A moduli stack with its grading is the accurate modern home for the informal quotient picture.
fate: The coordinate action is recorded in Morava's unpublished announcement communicated on 22 November 1972 \citep{morava1972moduli}. Its comodule geometry appears in the published \citet[Sections 0.1 and 1.0]{morava1985noetherian}; Johnson--Wilson's 1975 paper already develops substantial parts of the programme.
present_status: As of November 2026, the comodule and descent interpretation is established. The word ``constant'' is valid only in the weak sense of isomorphic fibres after choosing transport.

title: Height classifies geometric orbits in fixed positive characteristic
notes: Orbits \(\mathcal D_{(p,h)}\) for primes \(p\) and heights \(h\), together with an infinite-height stratum, are proposed. The theory is said to depend on describing these orbits.
statement: Over a fixed algebraically closed field \(k\) of characteristic \(p>0\), one-dimensional commutative formal groups are classified up to isomorphism by height \(h\in\{1,2,\ldots,\infty\}\), defined by the first nonzero term of \([p]_F(x)\), of degree \(p^h\); infinite height means \([p]_F=0\). The closure of the height-\(h\) stratum consists of heights at least \(h\). In characteristic zero all such groups become isomorphic to the additive group over a field. These are fibrewise orbit statements, not a claim that all points over \(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z\) lie in just three orbits.
reconstruction: The algebraic closure and fixed characteristic are indispensable. Arithmetic forms over smaller fields require additional descent data.
fate: The elementary height classification rests on older formal-group theory \citep{lazard1955formal}. The geometric stratification is exactly \citet[Theorem 1]{morava1972moduli}, an unpublished two-page announcement rather than a 1972 journal article; later published support includes \citet[Corollary 1.10]{johnsonwilson1975operations}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the height stratification and invariant-prime picture are established. The orbit geometry must be read with its stated base field.

title: Morava K-theories and the advertised periodicity
notes: The notes announce functors \(K(h)\), with periodicity \(2(p^h-1)\), and describe an infinite-height fibre as ordinary integral cohomology.
statement: For each prime \(p\) and integer \(h\geq1\), Morava \(K\)-theory is a homology theory with coefficient ring \(K(h)_*=\mathbb F_p[v_h^{\pm1}]\), \(|v_h|=2(p^h-1)\). Multiplication by \(v_h\) is the stated periodicity. Its construction cannot in general be replaced by the naive tensor product \(MU_*(X)\otimes_{MU_*}K(h)_*\). The additive formal group is represented by ordinary cohomology with the chosen coefficients; an infinite-height point in characteristic \(p\) gives a mod-\(p\) formal group, not automatically integral cohomology.
reconstruction: The coefficient field, grading and distinction between a constructed homology theory and an underived fibre are supplied. The notebook's \(\mathbb Z_p\) notation is not assumed to distinguish \(p\)-adic integers from integers modulo \(p\).
fate: \citet[Introduction, Sections 2--3]{johnsonwilson1975operations} constructs these theories and gives the coefficient ring and period explicitly. Its references identify Morava's Columbia notes as unpublished in 1971; this is earlier circulation distinct from the 1975 publication.
present_status: As of November 2026, Morava \(K\)-theories and the periodicity are established. Their heightwise relation to complex bordism has precise hypotheses, not the universal fibre identity suggested by the sketch.

title: Height stabilizers and p-adic division algebras
notes: Adams-type operations are indexed by units in a \(p\)-adic division algebra of dimension \(h^2\), described as the stabilizer of a point of a height orbit.
statement: For a height-\(h\) one-dimensional formal group over an algebraic closure of \(\mathbb F_p\), its automorphism group is the unit group \(\mathcal O_D^\times\) of the maximal order in the central division algebra \(D/\mathbb Q_p\) of invariant \(1/h\), with \(\dim_{\mathbb Q_p}D=h^2\). The full group \(D^\times\) allows quasi-isogenies and is larger. Stabilizer actions on height-theoretic objects require the chosen coefficient extension and realization; the notebook does not construct every asserted operation.
reconstruction: Units of the maximal order are distinguished from all nonzero division-algebra elements. The stabilizer identification is verified separately from the stronger claim of an action on a particular integral or mod-\(p\) cohomology theory.
fate: The precise stabilizer is \citet[Theorem 2]{morava1972moduli}; the November 1972 announcement remained unpublished and was later made available from archival material. Morava's published comodule theory gives the broader realization framework \citep{morava1985noetherian}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the stabilizer identification is established. A literal \(D^\times\)-action by automorphisms of the formal group would be too large.

title: Formal group laws and the Lazard–Quillen universal ring
notes: A one-dimensional commutative formal group law satisfies symmetry, a zero identity and associativity; the inverse exists automatically. The functor of such laws is represented by \(\Omega_U\).
statement: For a commutative ring \(R\), a formal group law is \(F(x,y)\in R[[x,y]]\) with \(F(x,0)=x\), \(F(0,y)=y\), associativity and commutativity. The linear terms are \(x+y\), so the inverse series is determined recursively. The functor of laws in a chosen coordinate is represented by the Lazard ring \(L\cong\mathbb Z[x_1,x_2,\ldots]\); Quillen identifies its universal law with the complex orientation law on \(MU_*\). The representing scheme classifies laws with coordinates, not isomorphism classes of formal groups.
reconstruction: The chosen coordinate is made explicit. Modding out coordinate changes leads to a stack rather than replacing the universal law ring by a ring of isomorphism classes.
fate: Representability is Lazard's 1955 theorem \citep{lazard1955formal}; the topological identification is \citet[Theorem 2]{quillen1969formal}, communicated in May and published in November 1969.
present_status: As of November 2026, the universal-property statement is established, with the distinction between laws and isomorphism classes.

title: Invariant differentials determine the logarithm over a Q-algebra
notes: Kazhdan's intervention says that in characteristic zero the invariant differential gives coordinates for the formal group; the coefficient of each power can be prescribed.
statement: Over a \(\mathbb Q\)-algebra \(R\), a normalized differential \(\omega=a(x)\,dx\), \(a(0)=1\), has a unique integral \(\ell(x)\in R[[x]]\) with \(\ell(0)=0\), \(\ell'(0)=1\). The law \(F(x,y)=\ell^{-1}(\ell(x)+\ell(y))\) has invariant differential \(\omega\). Thus normalized invariant differentials and commutative one-dimensional formal group laws are in bijection over \(\mathbb Q\)-algebras. Characteristic zero alone is insufficient for the integration argument: denominators may be absent, as in \(\mathbb Z\).
reconstruction: The \(\mathbb Q\)-algebra hypothesis replaces the weaker phrase characteristic zero. The claim is about a chosen coordinate and a normalized differential.
fate: The formula and the necessary rationalization are explicit in \citet[Section 1, formulas (1)--(2)]{quillen1969formal}. Morava returns to it on 14 April.
present_status: As of November 2026, the rational classification is established; integral formal groups retain information not removed by a logarithm over the original ring.
speaker: D. A. Kazhdan

title: Ramanujan’s tau function and the missing leading factor
notes: The notebook writes \(\prod_{m=1}^{\infty}(1-x^m)^{24}=\eta^{24}(x)=\sum_{n\geq1}\tau(n)x^n\). The first lower index is faint in transcription, but the scan and Dyson's original use \(m=1\).
statement: For \(\tau\) in the complex upper half-plane set \(q=e^{2\pi i\tau}\) and \(\eta(\tau)=q^{1/24}\prod_{m\geq1}(1-q^m)\). Ramanujan's integers are defined by \[\Delta(q)=\eta(\tau)^{24}=q\prod_{m\geq1}(1-q^m)^{24}=\sum_{n\geq1}\tau(n)q^n.\] The product without \(q\) has constant term 1 and coefficients \(\tau(n+1)\) at \(q^n\).
reconstruction: The variable \(q\), the upper-half-plane parameter and the leading factor are restored. The notebook conflates the eta function with its product part; this is not repaired by changing the convention for \(\tau(1)=1\).
fate: The normalization appears explicitly in \citet[equation (1), p. 636]{dyson1972missed}. Dyson delivered the lecture in January 1972; the journal text appeared in September. The missing factor is therefore a notebook error, not a later change of definition.
present_status: As of November 2026, the normalization is standard. Its correction follows already by comparing constant terms and is also required by the independent coefficient verification in this chapter.

title: Dyson’s five-variable lattice formula for tau
notes: The notes sum a ten-factor Vandermonde product over integers \(a,b,c,d,e\) satisfying residues \(1,2,3,4,5\pmod5\), zero sum and square sum \(10n\), with denominator \(1!2!3!4!\).
statement: For every positive integer \(n\), put \(v=(a,b,c,d,e)\) and \(V(v)=\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq5}(v_i-v_j)\). Then \[\tau(n)=\frac1{288}\!\sum_{\substack{a\equiv1,\ b\equiv2,\ c\equiv3,\ d\equiv4,\ e\equiv0\ (5)\\ a+b+c+d+e=0\\ a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2+e^2=10n}}\! V(a,b,c,d,e).\] Each coordinate is labelled by its residue class; the sum is not divided by an additional permutation factor.
reconstruction: Residue 5 is written as residue 0, and the denominator is evaluated. The formula has been checked editorially by three exact-integer algorithms for \(1\leq n\leq100\); the computational appendix marks this as \oursComputed{} and does not infer an all-\(n\) proof from the finite check.
fate: The exact identity is \citet[equation (2), p. 636]{dyson1972missed}, already in the January 1972 lecture. Its Lie-theoretic setting is the affine denominator identities discussed by \citet{macdonald1972affine}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the identity is established. The notebook's residue order, square-sum scale and denominator agree with the primary formula; the error lies in the preceding generating function, not in this lattice sum.

title: Eta powers and products over positive roots
notes: The exponents \(3,8,10,14,15,21,24,26,28,35,36\) are compared with dimensions of simple Lie algebras. The numerator of the tau formula is described as a product over ``simple roots (positive)'' of \(SL(5)\).
statement: The root system \(A_4\) has ten positive roots \(e_i-e_j\), \(i<j\), and only four simple roots. Evaluating the product over all positive roots gives the ten-factor Vandermonde in the formula above. The Lie-algebra dimensions \(\dim A_1=3\), \(\dim A_2=8\), \(\dim C_2=10\), \(\dim A_4=24\) illustrate the ordinary affine-denominator specializations. The exponent 26 is exceptional to this dimension list and must be considered separately.
reconstruction: ``Simple'' is deleted before ``positive roots''. A denominator-identity family is identified, without asserting that every eta-power identity is uniquely determined by the dimension of a simple Lie algebra.
fate: \citet[pp. 636--639]{dyson1972missed} describes the root-system discovery and Macdonald's general proof. The journal account \citep{macdonald1972affine} appeared in 1972, but the connection was already part of the January lecture summarized here.
present_status: As of November 2026, the root-system interpretation is established. Counting ten positive roots versus four simple roots provides an immediate internal check on the manuscript's wording.

title: Why does the exponent 26 occur?
notes: The exponent 26 is doubly underlined; Gelfand records that it ``drops out'' of the simple-Lie-algebra dimension pattern and remains unclear.
statement: Explain the eta-power identity with exponent 26 within the root-system framework, although 26 is not the dimension of a simple complex Lie algebra. The question concerns the structural source of that identity, not the existence of a simple Lie algebra of dimension 26.
reconstruction: The structural formulation follows the explicit contrast with the surrounding dimension list. No unspecified coefficient identity beyond the one discussed by Dyson is invented.
fate: \citet[Section I, pp. 200--201]{monastyrskii1980appendix} explains the exponent 26 through the dual-root construction associated with \(F_4\). The unequal root lengths lead to a specialization different from the ordinary dimension-52 pattern. This supplies a documented explanation of the notebook's exceptional exponent.
present_status: As of November 2026, the exceptional exponent is explained within affine root-system identities. It is not an unresolved problem and does not require a nonexistent 26-dimensional simple Lie algebra.

title: Limits of the kinematical groups
notes: The second example consists of \(c\to0\), \(c\to\infty\) and \(R\to\infty\), called limiting transitions in the kinematical group.
statement: A Lie-algebra contraction chooses invertible linear changes of basis depending on a parameter and takes a finite limit of the transformed structure constants. In the Poincar\'e algebra, normalize boosts by \([K_i,H]=P_i\), \([K_i,P_j]=\delta_{ij}H/c^2\) and \([K_i,K_j]=-\epsilon_{ijk}J_k/c^2\). The limit \(c\to\infty\) gives the Galilei brackets. For \(c\to0\), first set \(C_i=c^2K_i\); then \([C_i,P_j]=\delta_{ij}H\) survives while \([C_i,H]\) and \([C_i,C_j]\) vanish, giving the Carroll limit. Vanishing curvature \(R^{-2}\) contracts a de Sitter algebra to the Poincar\'e algebra.
reconstruction: The changes of basis and bracket normalizations are supplied to make the shorthand meaningful; limits of groups without specifying coordinates or rescaling are ambiguous. We do not reconstruct a complete classification from this one line.
fate: These are precisely the three processes discussed by \citet[Section 4, pp. 642--643]{dyson1972missed}, which cites Bacry and L\'evy-Leblond's 1968 analysis. Both the contraction method and these examples predate the seminar.
present_status: As of November 2026, the contractions are established examples. The excerpt contains no separate conjecture about physical applicability or an unproved classification.

title: Kirillov’s recap of bordism cycles over a space
notes: Under the heading ``Kirillov (recapitulation)'', a cycle is a quadruple \((M,\xi,\alpha,f)\): \(M\) is a compact weakly complex manifold, \(\alpha\) is a specified stable tangent-bundle isomorphism, and \(f:M\to X\). A diagram gives the extending bundle and map on a bordism.
statement: For a CW space \(X\), a geometric complex-bordism cycle consists of a closed smooth manifold with a chosen stable complex structure and a continuous map to \(X\). Two cycles are equivalent when their disjoint union with the opposite bordism structure bounds a compact manifold whose stable complex structure and map extend the boundary data. Disjoint union and Cartesian products give \(MU_*(X)\) its graded \(MU_*\)-module structure.
reconstruction: ``Weak complex set'' in the translation is read as a stably complex manifold. The stable isomorphism is part of the structure and must extend; existence of a complex bundle with the same stable real class alone does not specify a cycle.
fate: This repeats the established geometric construction in 1971-268.1 and 1971-268.4; its pre-seminar context is \citet{connerfloyd1966relation}. The recurrence is an exposition, not a second proposed theory.
present_status: As of November 2026, the geometric model and module action are standard. This entry records Kirillov's intervention separately from Morava's later assertions.
speaker: A. A. Kirillov

title: The coefficient ring and the affine sheaf attached to bordism
notes: The coefficient theorem is now written \(A=\Omega_*^U(*)=\mathbb Z[t_1,t_2,\ldots]\), \(\deg t_i=2i\), with \(t_1\leftrightarrow\mathbb {CP}^1\). The module \(M=\Omega_*^U(X)\) gives a sheaf over \(\mathbb A=\operatorname{Spec}A\).
statement: Complex bordism has coefficient ring \(MU_*\cong\mathbb Z[x_1,x_2,\ldots]\), with \(|x_i|=2i\), and a degree-two generator may be chosen as \([\mathbb {CP}^1]\). Any module \(M\) defines a quasicoherent sheaf \(\widetilde M\) on \(\operatorname{Spec}MU_*\), after forgetting or separately recording its grading. The infinitely generated polynomial coefficient ring is not noetherian.
reconstruction: This page correctly starts the polynomial generators at index 1, unlike P000441. The nonnoetherian qualification matters when comparing the later finite-type homogeneous-space assertion with the infinite formal-group scheme.
fate: The coefficient theorem and identification with the universal formal-group ring are explicit in \citet[Theorem 2]{quillen1969formal}; the associated-sheaf construction is standard affine algebraic geometry. Morava's equivariant version is developed in \citet[Section 1.0]{morava1985noetherian}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the coefficient and sheaf constructions are established. They do not by themselves identify the fibres with familiar integral cohomology theories.
speaker: A. A. Kirillov

title: The three orbit types and the proposed fibre theories
notes: There is said to be one dense open orbit, one closed orbit and countably many intermediate orbits; their fibres are labelled \(K(X)\), \(H^*(X,\mathbb Z)\), and \(K(n)(X,\mathbb Z_p)\). The intermediate labels also involve the prime \(p\).
statement: Over an algebraically closed field of a fixed positive characteristic \(p\), coordinate-change orbits of one-dimensional commutative formal groups are indexed by heights \(1,2,\ldots,\infty\): height 1 is open, infinite height is closed, and finite higher heights lie between them. The positive finite-height cohomology theories are Morava \(K(h)\), with coefficients \(\mathbb F_p[v_h^{\pm1}]\), \(|v_h|=2(p^h-1)\). These are not a literal classification into three orbits over \(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z\), nor are all their geometric fibres integral \(K\)-groups or integral ordinary cohomology.
reconstruction: The orbit theorem is restricted to a fixed algebraically closed base field. The labels of homology theories are separated from raw tensor-product fibres, repeating the corrections in 1971-268.6--1971-268.9. No claim is made that the fibre alone defines a generalized homology theory for every space.
fate: The geometric orbit theorem is \citet[Theorem 1]{morava1972moduli}, an unpublished November 1972 announcement. The coefficient rings and realization of the periodic theories are treated in \citet[Introduction and Sections 2--3]{johnsonwilson1975operations}, citing Morava's unpublished 1971 work.
present_status: As of November 2026, the height picture and the periodic theories are established. The global integral-fibre formulation remains false as written, and is not an open problem.

title: The fibre M/MJ and the residue field
notes: A point \((a_1,a_2,\ldots)\) gives a purported maximal ideal \(J=(t_1-a_1,t_2-a_2,\ldots)\). The fibre is \(M/MJ\), called a vector space and then more accurately an \(A/J\)-module.
